claim: In eukaryotes, intra-chromosomal recombination generates DNA circles.
source: In eukaryotes, intra-chromosomal recombination generates DNA circles, but little is known about how cells react to them.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about eukaryotic biology.

claim: The SAGA complex mediates the interaction of non-chromosomal DNA circles with nuclear pore complexes (NPCs).
source: In this study, we show that the SAGA complex mediates the interaction of non-chromosomal DNA circles with nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) and thereby promotes their confinement in the mother cell.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study as stated in the abstract.

claim: SAGA-mediated interaction of DNA circles with NPCs promotes confinement of circles in the mother cell.
source: In this study, we show that the SAGA complex mediates the interaction of non-chromosomal DNA circles with nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) and thereby promotes their confinement in the mother cell.
evidence: This is stated as a direct consequence of SAGA-mediated interaction in the abstract.

claim: SAGA-mediated retention of DNA circles causes retention and accumulation of NPCs in mother cells.
source: Reciprocally, this causes retention and accumulation of NPCs, which affects the organization of ageing nuclei.
evidence: This is stated as a reciprocal effect in the abstract.

claim: Accumulation of circles and NPCs in the mother cell promotes ageing.
source: Thus, SAGA prevents the spreading of DNA circles by linking them to NPCs, but unavoidably causes accumulation of circles and NPCs in the mother cell, and thereby promotes ageing.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the abstract.

claim: When recombination occurs between two loci on the same chromosome, recombination is intra-chromosomal.
source: However, when recombination occurs between two loci on the same chromosome, i.e. if the break affects a repeated region of the genome, recombination is intra-chromosomal.
evidence: This is stated as a definition in the introduction.

claim: In 50% of intra-chromosomal recombination events, the resolution of the Holliday junction leads to the excision of a DNA circle.
source: In 50% of these events, the resolution of the Holliday junction leads to the excision of a DNA circle containing one or several of the involved repeats (Gaubatz, 1990).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: rDNA circles have been found in all eukaryotes tested so far.
source: Accordingly, due to the highly repeated nature of the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, rDNA circles have been found in all eukaryotes tested so far (Cohen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) form spontaneously.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) form spontaneously but fail to accumulate in the population, owing to their highly asymmetric segregation upon cell division (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: ERCs fail to accumulate in the yeast population due to their highly asymmetric segregation upon cell division.
source: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) form spontaneously but fail to accumulate in the population, owing to their highly asymmetric segregation upon cell division (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: rDNA circles contain a replication origin and duplicate in S-phase.
source: Since rDNA circles contain a replication origin they duplicate in S-phase, and due to the asymmetric segregation they accumulate with time in the mother cell.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of rDNA circles.

claim: rDNA circles accumulate with time in the mother cell due to asymmetric segregation.
source: Since rDNA circles contain a replication origin they duplicate in S-phase, and due to the asymmetric segregation they accumulate with time in the mother cell.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of replication and asymmetric segregation.

claim: Artificially introducing an ERC into the bud reduces its life span.
source: Artificially introducing an ERC into the bud reduces its life span (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mutations that enhance ERC formation shorten the longevity of mother cells.
source: Likewise, mutations that enhance ERC formation shorten the longevity of mother cells (Kaeberlein et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: fob1∆ mutant cells live longer than wild-type cells.
source: Conversely, mutant cells with reduced rates of ERC formation, such as fob1∆, or those defective in ERC retention, such as bud6∆ mutant cells, live longer (Defossez et al., 1999; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: bud6∆ mutant cells live longer than wild-type cells.
source: Conversely, mutant cells with reduced rates of ERC formation, such as fob1∆, or those defective in ERC retention, such as bud6∆ mutant cells, live longer (Defossez et al., 1999; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: Any artificial circle that replicates in vivo but lacks a partitioning sequence segregates asymmetrically.
source: Interestingly, any artificial circle that replicates in vivo but lacks a partitioning sequence (e.g. a centromere) segregates similarly and promotes replicative ageing when introduced into yeast (Falcon and Aris, 2003).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Non-chromosomal DNA circles segregate asymmetrically in a manner that is independent of their DNA sequence.
source: Thus, non-chromosomal DNA circles segregate asymmetrically, affect cellular physiology, and promote ageing in a manner that is independent of their DNA sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from previous observations.

claim: The morpho-kinetic model proposes that circles freely diffuse in the nucleus and their retention results from nuclear morphology and short anaphase duration.
source: The morpho-kinetic model proposes that circles freely diffuse in the nucleus and that their retention results from the morphology of the dividing yeast nucleus and the short duration of anaphase, which together limit the probability that DNA circles diffuse into the bud (Gehlen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as a description of an existing model with citation.

claim: The morpho-kinetic model predicts a retention frequency of 0.75–0.90 per individual plasmid.
source: Using measured parameters for nuclear geometry and division speed, this model predicts a retention frequency of 0.75–0.90 per individual plasmid.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the morpho-kinetic model.

claim: Mathematical modeling indicates that observed ageing curves require retention frequencies above 0.99 per individual ERC.
source: However, mathematical modeling indicates that observed ageing curves require retention frequencies above 0.99 per individual ERC (Gillespie et al., 2004), which is higher than what the morpho-kinetic model can achieve.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A lateral diffusion barrier in the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope impedes the diffusion of membrane proteins through the bud neck.
source: A second model, the barrier model, is based on the observation that a lateral diffusion barrier in the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope impedes the diffusion of membrane proteins through the bud neck and hence their exchange between mother and bud parts of the nucleus (Shcheprova et al., 2008; Boettcher et al., 2012; Clay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to support the claim.

claim: The barrier model proposes that DNA circles attach to a receptor in the nuclear envelope to ensure their confinement into the mother cell.
source: This model proposes that DNA circles attach to a receptor in the nuclear envelope to ensure their subsequent confinement into the mother cell by the lateral diffusion barrier (Shcheprova et al., 2008; Clay et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the barrier model with citations.

claim: 3 hours after centromere excision, plasmids are localized away from the SPBs in 68% of the cells.
source: 3 hr after addition of estradiol to induce centromere excision, plasmids are localized away from the SPBs in 68% of the cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: Most cells with plasmids away from SPBs displayed one or two small plasmid foci (61% or 33%, respectively).
source: Most of those cells displayed one or two small plasmid foci (61% or 33%, respectively; Figure 1A) and only 6% of the cells showed more than two foci.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Plasmid foci were on average 2.5 times more intense than the nucleoplasmic background.
source: These foci were on average 2.5 times more intense than the nucleoplasmic background (Figure 1B) and localized to the vicinity of the nuclear rim (see below, and Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to figures.

claim: After 16-18 hours in selective media, 93% of cells contained no plasmid.
source: In contrast, when the cells were grown in selective media for 16–18 hr, allowing the circles to accumulate through multiple rounds of replication and division, the majority of the cells (93%) contained no plasmid, consistent with the plasmids segregating asymmetrically and accumulating in only few retaining cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: After 16-18 hours in selective media, 6% of cells carried one large and intense plasmid signal, 8-fold above background.
source: A small fraction of the cells (1%) contained few plasmids visualized as small foci as above, whereas the rest of the cells (6%) carried one large and intense signal, 8-fold above background (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Cells with fluorescent plasmid mass had 5.2 ± 1.9 bud scars compared to 0.7 ± 0.9 bud scars in cells without plasmids.
source: Consistent with the idea that this fluorescent mass corresponded to the accumulated plasmids, these cells were the few initial mother cells that had already proceeded through several division cycles, as determined by the visualization of bud scars with calcofluor white (5.2 ± 1.9 bud scars on cells with fluorescent mass compared to 0.7 ± 0.9 bud scars in cells without plasmids).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: Accumulated plasmids did not spread throughout the nucleoplasm but were collected to a single place at the nuclear periphery.
source: Remarkably, these accumulated plasmids did not spread throughout the nucleoplasm but rather were collected to a single place at the nuclear periphery.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments.

claim: Nuclei loaded with DNA circles were larger than those with no or few circles (average volume increased 1.7-fold).
source: Labeling of the nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) indicated that the nuclei loaded with DNA circles were larger than those with no or few circles (average volume increased 1.7-fold; N = 50 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: Circle-loaded cells contained on average 2.7-fold more nuclear pores compared to cells without plasmids.
source: Remarkably, accumulation of DNA circles drastically affected the NPC distribution. The circle-loaded cells contained on an average 2.7-fold more nuclear pores compared to cells without plasmids (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: The increase in NPCs was independent of the NPC reporter used (Nup82-3sfGFP: 2.7-fold, Nup82-GFP: 2.6-fold, Nup49-GFP: 3.0-fold).
source: This increase was independent of the NPC reporter used (Nup82-3sfGFP, 2.7-folds, N = 50 cells; Nup82-GFP, 2.6-fold, N = 25 cells; Nup49-GFP, 3.0-fold, N = 25 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 1C) and was exclusively observed in the cells that contained DNA circles.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: All circle-loaded cells exhibited an NPC cap that covered the DNA circles.
source: Most strikingly, NPC distribution over the nuclear envelope was no-longer uniform; a substantial fraction of the NPCs accumulated in a single cap that covered one side of the nucleus (Figure 1A,C). In all cells, this cap covered the DNA circles. Furthermore, all circle-loaded cells exhibited such a cap.
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to figures.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of Nup82-3sfGFP was on average two-fold higher in the vicinity of the circles compared with the rest of the nucleus.
source: As a consequence, the fluorescence intensity of Nup82-3sfGFP was on an average two-fold higher in the vicinity of the circles (Ic = 2.02 ± 0.80 A.U.) compared with the rest of the nucleus (Ir = 1.0 ± 0.35 A.U., N = 50 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: In time-lapse movies, the NPC cap and the mCherry patch moved together.
source: In time-lapse movies (5 min intervals for 60 min), the cap and the mCherry patch moved together (Figure 1E, Video 1), suggesting that DNA circles and the NPC cap were linked to each other.
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse microscopy with reference to figure and video.

claim: The asymmetry in nuclear size during division was enhanced in cells with accumulated circles.
source: While all dividing cells formed two daughter nuclei of different sizes, the mother nucleus being generally larger, this asymmetry was enhanced in cells with accumulated circles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: The density of NPCs was increased in mother nuclei of cells with accumulated circles.
source: Furthermore, the density of NPCs was increased in these mother nuclei (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Mother cells containing accumulated plasmids retained a larger fraction of their NPCs (median = 78%) compared to cells containing no circles (63%).
source: Mother cells containing accumulated plasmids retained a larger fraction of their NPCs (median = 78%, N = 50), compared to cells containing no circles (63%, N = 50 cells, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: In cells with accumulated plasmids, both the TetR-mCherry signal and the GFP cap localized to the vicinity of the nuclear bridge on its mother side.
source: Interestingly, in these cells both the TetR-mCherry signal and the GFP cap localized to the vicinity of the nuclear bridge linking mother and bud lobes of the dividing nucleus on its mother side (Figures 1A and 2A and Video 1).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to figures and video.

claim: Only in very rare cases (2%) a fraction of the plasmid mass passed to the bud.
source: Only in very rare cases a fraction of the plasmid mass passed to the bud (2%, N > 50 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: In bud6∆ cells, the NPC cap still formed around the plasmid.
source: In cells lacking Bud6, the NPC cap still formed around the plasmid leading to an increase in NPC signal in the circle area (Ic = 2.29 ± 0.67 A.U.) compared to the residual area (Ir = 1.0 ± 0.33 A.U., N = 50 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: In bud6∆ cells, 11% of cells transmitted part of the plasmid mass to the daughter cell (compared to 2% in wild-type cells).
source: However, in 11% of the cells, part of the plasmid mass was transmitted to the daughter cell (compared to 2% in wild-type cells, N = 50 cells).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: Retention of the circles and the NPC cap partially depends on the lateral diffusion barrier.
source: Thus, retention of the circles and the NPC cap partially depends on the lateral diffusion barrier separating the mother and bud parts of the nuclear envelope.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the bud6∆ experiments.

claim: In wild-type cells, non-centromeric circles rarely passed to the daughter cells (pf = 3.9 ± 1.1).
source: In wild-type cells, non-centromeric circles rarely passed to the daughter cells (pf = 3.9 ± 1.1; Figure 3A), that is 2.5- to 4-fold less frequently than predicted by the passive model (pf = 10–15; (Gehlen et al., 2011)).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Circle propagation into the bud was significantly increased in yku70∆ cells (pf = 10.3 ± 1.3).
source: Circle propagation into the bud was significantly increased in yku70∆ and bud6∆ cells, as previously reported ((Shcheprova et al., 2008; Gehlen et al., 2011); pf = 10.3 ± 1.3 and 11.8 ± 0.8, respectively, N = 3 clones, >50 cells each, p < 0.001; Figure 3A), validating our approach.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure and citations.

claim: Circle propagation into the bud was significantly increased in bud6∆ cells (pf = 11.8 ± 0.8).
source: Circle propagation into the bud was significantly increased in yku70∆ and bud6∆ cells, as previously reported ((Shcheprova et al., 2008; Gehlen et al., 2011); pf = 10.3 ± 1.3 and 11.8 ± 0.8, respectively, N = 3 clones, >50 cells each, p < 0.001; Figure 3A), validating our approach.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure and citations.

claim: Cells lacking Gcn5 showed a clear increase in plasmid propagation (pf = 11.1 ± 2.8).
source: In contrast, cells lacking Gcn5, a component of the Spt-Ada-Gcn5 acetyltransferase (SAGA) complex, showed a clear increase in plasmid propagation (pf = 11.1 ± 2.8, N = 3 clones, >100 cells each, p < 0.001), similar to the defect observed in bud6∆ mutant cells and fitting well with propagation frequencies predicted by the passive model.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: All SAGA mutants tested (spt3Δ and sgf73Δ) displayed similar defects in DNA circle retention.
source: All SAGA mutants tested, including spt3Δ and sgf73Δ, displayed similar defects in DNA circle retention (pf = 9.7 ± 1.7 and 11.8 ± 1.6, respectively, N = 3 clones, >50 cells each, p < 0.001; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Replacement of GCN5 with the point mutant allele gcn5-E173A led to a similar increase in plasmid propagation (pf = 11.0 ± 1.5).
source: Furthermore, replacement of the GCN5 gene with a point mutant allele abrogating its acetyl-ransferase activity, gcn5-E173A (Wang et al., 1998) led to a similar increase in plasmid propagation to the daughter cell as observed in gcn5Δ mutant cells (pf = 11.0 ± 1.5, N = 3 clones, >100 cells each, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with citation.

claim: SAGA and its acetyl-transferase activity promote the retention of DNA circles in the mother cell.
source: Thus, SAGA and its acetyl–transferase activity, which are known to link chromatin to NPCs, promote the retention of DNA circles in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SAGA mutant experiments.

claim: In 38% (±6%) of wild-type cells, all ERCs remained in the mother cell.
source: In 38% (±6%) of the wild-type cells, all ERCs that had accumulated in the mother cell remained in the mother cell, as demonstrated by the fact that their daughters lacked the ADE2 marker and formed a red colony (see material and methods, (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997)).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with citation.

claim: The percentage of cells retaining all ERCs was reduced 2.5-fold in gcn5∆ and sgf73∆ mutant cells (16 ± 2% and 15 ± 2%).
source: This percentage was reduced 2.5-fold in the gcn5∆ and the sgf73∆ single mutant cells (16 ± 2% and 15 ± 2%, N ≥ 3 clones, p < 0.001; Figure 3B), indicating that high-fidelity retention of ERCs in the mother cell requires SAGA function.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: SAGA mutant cells of the same age as wild-type contained fewer ERCs.
source: While no ERCs were detected in young wild-type cells, substantial ERC accumulation was observed in aged wild-type mothers. In contrast, SAGA mutant cells of the same age contained fewer ERCs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from Southern blot experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: The rate of ERC formation was decreased 2-fold in sgf73∆ cells.
source: By scoring the frequency of half sectored colonies, we observed that the rate of ERC formation was decreased 2 folds in the sgf73∆, similar but less pronounced to what McCormick et al. (2014) reported (Figure 3D and (McCormick et al., 2014)).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: ERC formation increased 1.5-fold in gcn5∆ mutant cells.
source: However, ERC formation increased 1.5-fold in gcn5∆ mutant cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: In gcn5∆ mutant mother cells, the slow rate of ERC accumulation results from the failure in their retention rather than reduced ERC formation.
source: Together, these results indicate that, at least in the gcn5∆ mutant mother cells, the slow rate of ERC accumulation results from the failure in their retention rather than reduced ERC formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ERC formation and accumulation experiments.

claim: Deleting YKU70 prolonged anaphase.
source: Measuring anaphase duration using time lapse movies of cells expressing Nsg1-GFP revealed that deleting YKU70 prolonged anaphase, as expected (Gehlen et al., 2011), whereas deletion of BUD6, GCN5, or SGF73 did not (N ≥ 180 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse microscopy experiments with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Deletion of BUD6, GCN5, or SGF73 did not affect anaphase duration.
source: Measuring anaphase duration using time lapse movies of cells expressing Nsg1-GFP revealed that deleting YKU70 prolonged anaphase, as expected (Gehlen et al., 2011), whereas deletion of BUD6, GCN5, or SGF73 did not (N ≥ 180 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from time-lapse microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Nuclear bridges were not wider in gcn5∆ cells.
source: Furthermore, nuclear bridges were not wider in gcn5∆ cells (N ≥ 70 cells; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: The bud6∆ mutation reduced compartmentalization of the envelope.
source: Although the bud6∆ mutation reduced compartmentalization of the envelope, as reported previously (Shcheprova et al., 2008), no effect was observed in gcn5∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type cells (N ≥ 20 cells; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from FLIP experiments with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: No effect on the diffusion barrier was observed in gcn5∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: Although the bud6∆ mutation reduced compartmentalization of the envelope, as reported previously (Shcheprova et al., 2008), no effect was observed in gcn5∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type cells (N ≥ 20 cells; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from FLIP experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: SAGA does not affect nuclear geometry, anaphase duration, and the diffusion barrier.
source: Thus, SAGA does not affect nuclear geometry, anaphase duration, and the diffusion barrier. Therefore SAGA must play a different role in circle retention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments testing these parameters.

claim: Inactivation of the core TREX-2 gene SAC3 caused circles to propagate to the bud 3 times more frequently than in wild-type cells (pf = 11.5 ± 3.0).
source: Thus, we examined whether TREX-2 also contributed to circle retention. Inactivation of the core TREX-2 gene, SAC3, caused circles to propagate to the bud 3 times more frequently than in wild-type cells, i.e. at a frequency similar to SAGA defective cells (pf = 11.5 ± 3.0, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Deletion of SUS1 led to similar effects on circle propagation as deletion of SAC3 (pf = 11.3 ± 1.4).
source: Deletion of SUS1, which inactivates both SAGA and TREX-2 complexes (Pascual-Garcia and Rodriguez-Navarro, 2009), and deleting both the GCN5 and SAC3 genes led to similar effects (pf = 11.3 ± 1.4, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001 and pf = 11.1 ± 1.3, N = 3 clones p < 0.001, respectively), indicating that the effects of inactivating SAGA and TREX-2 were not additive.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with citation.

claim: The effects of inactivating SAGA and TREX-2 were not additive.
source: Deletion of SUS1, which inactivates both SAGA and TREX-2 complexes (Pascual-Garcia and Rodriguez-Navarro, 2009), and deleting both the GCN5 and SAC3 genes led to similar effects (pf = 11.3 ± 1.4, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001 and pf = 11.1 ± 1.3, N = 3 clones p < 0.001, respectively), indicating that the effects of inactivating SAGA and TREX-2 were not additive.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments.

claim: The SAGA complex and the NPC component TREX-2 act together in a pathway mediating the targeted retention of non-chromosomal circles in the mother cell.
source: We conclude that the SAGA complex and the NPC component TREX-2 act together in a pathway mediating the targeted retention of non-chromosomal circles in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the genetic experiments.

claim: Only 15% (±2.8%) of plasmid foci were at a resolvable distance from the nuclear envelope in wild-type cells.
source: Consistent with this idea, the vast majority of non-centromeric circles localized to the nuclear rim in wild-type cells: only 15% (±2.8%) of plasmid foci were at a resolvable distance from the nuclear envelope (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: In gcn5∆ mutant cells, 31.9% (±1.3%) of plasmid foci were at a resolvable distance from the nuclear envelope.
source: In contrast, this fraction was substantially increased in cells lacking SAGA (gcn5∆ mutant cells) or both SAGA and TREX-2 function (sus1∆ mutant cells; 31.9% ± 1.3% and 24.1% ± 2.6%, respectively, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: In sus1∆ mutant cells, 24.1% (±2.6%) of plasmid foci were at a resolvable distance from the nuclear envelope.
source: In contrast, this fraction was substantially increased in cells lacking SAGA (gcn5∆ mutant cells) or both SAGA and TREX-2 function (sus1∆ mutant cells; 31.9% ± 1.3% and 24.1% ± 2.6%, respectively, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: The average Nup82-3sfGFP intensity increased in the vicinity of the circle by +33.2% (±0.09%) in wild-type cells.
source: Aligning all traces with the position of the DNA circle showed that the average Nup82-3sfGFP intensity increased in the vicinity of the circle compared to elsewhere (+33.2% ± 0.09%, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: No increase in nuclear pore signal was observed near DNA circles in gcn5∆ and sus1∆ mutant cells.
source: No such increase in nuclear pore signal was observed near DNA circles in gcn5∆ and sus1∆ mutant cells (+4.6% ± 0.05% and −2.0% ± 0.07%, p < 0.01).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: SAGA promotes the interaction of non-chromosomal DNA circles to nuclear pores.
source: Thus, we conclude that SAGA indeed promotes the interaction of non-chromosomal DNA circles to nuclear pores.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the localization experiments.

claim: Nup170-TetR fusion protein had no effect on circle retention in wild-type cells (pf = 5.5 ± 0.7).
source: Neither fusion protein had any effect on circle retention when replacing the corresponding endogenous nucleoporin in otherwise wild-type cells (pf = 5.5 ± 0.7 in NUP170-TetR and 4.6 ± 1.6 in NUP49-TetR cells; Figure 6A), as reported.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Nup49-TetR fusion protein had no effect on circle retention in wild-type cells (pf = 4.6 ± 1.6).
source: Neither fusion protein had any effect on circle retention when replacing the corresponding endogenous nucleoporin in otherwise wild-type cells (pf = 5.5 ± 0.7 in NUP170-TetR and 4.6 ± 1.6 in NUP49-TetR cells; Figure 6A), as reported.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: When expressed in gcn5∆, sgf73∆, or sus1∆ mutant cells, Nup170-TetR and Nup49-TetR fusion proteins restored the retention of the reporter circle in the mother cell fully or largely so.
source: In contrast, when expressed in gcn5∆, sgf73∆, or sus1∆ mutant cells, these fusion proteins restored the retention of the reporter circle in the mother cell fully or largely so.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Tethering of the circles to the nuclear pores did not bypass the requirement for the diffusion barrier in plasmid retention.
source: Importantly, tethering of the circles to the nuclear pores did not bypass the requirement for the diffusion barrier in plasmid retention, since bud6∆ mutant cells expressing Nup170 or Nup49 fused to TetR displayed plasmid propagation frequencies similar to bud6∆ cells (pf = 11.9 ± 1.8 and 10.8 ± 1.2, respectively; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Non-chromosomal DNA circles artificially tethered to NPCs no longer need SAGA for being efficiently retained in the mother cell by the diffusion barrier.
source: Thus, non-chromosomal DNA circles artificially tethered to NPCs no longer need SAGA for being efficiently retained in the mother cell by the diffusion barrier.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tethering experiments.

claim: Nup2 and Mlp1 diffuse more rapidly than the core nucleoporins Nup1, Nup49, and Nup170 during anaphase.
source: Accordingly, we found that both Nup2 and Mlp1, as well as Nup60, diffuse more rapidly than the core nucleoporins Nup1, Nup49, and Nup170, at least during anaphase (Figure 6C), indicating that their residence at NPCs is transitory.
evidence: This is an observation from FRAP experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: The stable association of nucleoporins with NPCs was highly correlated with their ability to mediate circle retention.
source: Remarkably, the stable association of nucleoporins with NPCs was highly correlated with their ability to mediate circle retention (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing FRAP and retention data with reference to a figure.

claim: Artificially attaching non-centromeric plasmids to NPC components bypasses the need for SAGA function, provided that the used nucleoporin is stable at NPCs.
source: Together, our data indicate that artificially attaching non-centromeric plasmids to NPC components bypasses the need for SAGA function, provided that the used nucleoporin is stable at NPCs. Thus, SAGA functions in retention through promoting stable anchorage of the circles to NPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the tethering and FRAP experiments.

claim: Expression of Gcn5-Sac3 fusion protein had no effect on plasmid retention in wild-type cells (pf = 5.2 ± 0.4).
source: Expression of either of these two fusion proteins had no effect on plasmid retention in otherwise wild-type cells (pf = 5.2 ± 0.4 and 4.1 ± 1.0, respectively; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Expression of Spt7-Nup49 fusion protein had no effect on plasmid retention in wild-type cells (pf = 4.1 ± 1.0).
source: Expression of either of these two fusion proteins had no effect on plasmid retention in otherwise wild-type cells (pf = 5.2 ± 0.4 and 4.1 ± 1.0, respectively; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Gcn5-Sac3 fusion protein largely bypassed the need for Sgf73 in circle retention (pf = 6.1 ± 1.3 compared to 11.8 ± 1.6 in sgf73∆ cells).
source: However, it largely bypassed the need for Sgf73 (pf = 6.1 ± 1.3 with Gcn5-Sac3 and 6.8 ± 2.0 with Spt7-Nup49, compared to 11.8 ± 1.6 in sgf73∆ cells) and Sus1 (pf = 6.5 ± 1.3 with Gcn5-Sac3 and 5.6 ± 0.2 with Spt7-Nup49, compared to 11.3 ± 1.4 in sus1∆ cells, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: Spt7-Nup49 fusion protein largely bypassed the need for Sgf73 in circle retention (pf = 6.8 ± 2.0 compared to 11.8 ± 1.6 in sgf73∆ cells).
source: However, it largely bypassed the need for Sgf73 (pf = 6.1 ± 1.3 with Gcn5-Sac3 and 6.8 ± 2.0 with Spt7-Nup49, compared to 11.8 ± 1.6 in sgf73∆ cells) and Sus1 (pf = 6.5 ± 1.3 with Gcn5-Sac3 and 5.6 ± 0.2 with Spt7-Nup49, compared to 11.3 ± 1.4 in sus1∆ cells, N = 3 clones, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments.

claim: The main function of Sgf73 and Sus1 in plasmid retention is to physically link SAGA to nuclear pores.
source: Thus, the main function of Sgf73 and Sus1 in plasmid retention is to physically link SAGA to nuclear pores. These data establish that SAGA needs to be at NPCs in order to function in circle retention.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fusion protein experiments.

claim: Both SAGA components Gcn5-GFP and Sgf73-GFP were strongly enriched in the plasmid area.
source: To address whether SAGA interacts with non-centromeric DNA circles, we then analyzed the localization of Gcn5-GFP and Sgf73-GFP fusion proteins in cells accumulating non-centromeric DNA circles labeled with TetR-mCherry. Both SAGA components were strongly enriched in the plasmid area, indicating that SAGA interacts more readily with non-chromosomal DNA than with the rest of the genome (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: ChIP experiments showed a clear enrichment of the SAGA proteins Gcn5 and Spt20 on a non-centromeric reporter plasmid.
source: Accordingly, chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) experiments (N = 5 independent experiments) reproducibly showed a clear enrichment of the SAGA proteins Gcn5 and Spt20 on a non-centromeric reporter plasmid (pYB1670/CEN-), as judged by probing for the autonomous replication sequence (ARS) and two non-coding sequences of bacterial origin.
evidence: This is an observation from ChIP experiments.

claim: SAGA enrichment on the plasmid was nearly lost when the same plasmid contained a centromere.
source: Strikingly, this enrichment was nearly lost (p < 0.05) when the same plasmid contained a centromere (CEN+; Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an observation from ChIP experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: SAGA is recruited to higher levels on non-centromeric than on centromeric DNA circles.
source: Thus, SAGA is recruited to higher levels on non-centromeric than on centromeric DNA circles. Together, these data indicate that SAGA more stably associates with non-chromosomal than with chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP experiments.

claim: Expression of Gcn5-TetR fusion protein reduced the propagation of the circle to the bud 3-fold compared to wild-type (pf = 1.1 ± 0.3).
source: We increased Gcn5 levels on our TetO circle through expression of a Gcn5-TetR fusion protein and asked whether this affected its retention. Strikingly, this construct reduced the propagation of the circle to the bud 3-fold compared to wild-type (pf = 1.1 ± 0.3; N = 3 clones, p < 0.001; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Cells expressing Sir2 fused to TetR segregated the circle to the bud as frequently as SAGA defective cells.
source: In contrast, cells expressing the deacetylase Sir2 fused to TetR segregated the circle to the bud as frequently as SAGA defective cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Binding of SAGA to the circle is required for efficient retention of the circle in the mother cell.
source: Thus, we concluded that binding of SAGA to the circle is required for efficient retention of the circle in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Gcn5-TetR and Sir2-TetR experiments.

claim: The accumulation of DNA circles had no effect on pore segregation in gcn5∆ and sgf73∆ single mutant cells.
source: In favor of this idea, and in contrast to what we observed in wild-type cells (Figure 2A), the accumulation of DNA circles had no effect on pore segregation in gcn5∆ and sgf73∆ single mutant cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to figures.

claim: SAGA-dependent attachment of the circles to pores promotes the retention not only of the circles but also of those NPCs.
source: Thus, SAGA-dependent attachment of the circles to pores promotes the retention not only of the circles but also of those NPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the NPC segregation experiments in SAGA mutants.

claim: In wild-type cells loaded with circles, the NPC signal decayed slower and to a lesser extent in regions associated with the circles (t70 = 82 ± 39 s) than in those on the opposite side (t70 = 25 ± 8 s).
source: When fluorescence intensity was measured both in the vicinity of the circles (Ic) and at opposite side of the nucleus (Io) in wild-type cells loaded with circles, with both measurement regions equidistant from the bleached spot, the signal decayed slower and to a lesser extent in regions associated with the circles (t70 = 82 ± 39 s) than in those on the opposite side (t70 = 25 ± 8 s, N = 20 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from FLIP experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: In SAGA deficient cells, circles did not cluster to one focus and the cells formed no NPC cap.
source: We could not perform the same experiment in SAGA deficient cells because circles did not cluster to one focus and the cells formed no NPC cap. NPC distribution remained uniform over the nuclear surface, and non-centromeric circles were scattered throughout the nucleoplasm (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is an observation from microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: SAGA mediates both circle clustering and the formation of the NPC cap.
source: We concluded that SAGA mediates both circle clustering and the formation of the NPC cap.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observations in SAGA deficient cells.

claim: SAGA-dependent attachment of non-centromeric DNA circles substantially reduces the mobility of the corresponding NPCs.
source: Thus, SAGA-dependent attachment of non-centromeric DNA circles substantially, and specifically, reduces the mobility of the corresponding NPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FLIP experiments.

claim: In circle-free exponentially growing cells only very few NPCs, if any, are stably attached to and slowed down by chromatin.
source: These data establish two points. First, in circle-free exponentially growing cells only very few NPCs, if any, are stably attached to and slowed down by chromatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FLIP experiments.

claim: NPCs that are attached to DNA circles show very slow dynamics, possibly explaining their enhanced retention in the mother cell during mitosis.
source: Second, NPCs that are attached to DNA circles show very slow dynamics, possibly explaining their enhanced retention in the mother cell during mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FLIP experiments.

claim: The average speed of DNA circles was significantly higher in cells lacking Gcn5 (0.09 ± 0.027 μm/s) than in wild-type cells (0.05 ± 0.019 μm/s).
source: In time-lapse movies (one stack every 3 s, 20 optical slices per stack, for 3 min), the average speed of the DNA circles was significantly higher in cells lacking Gcn5 (0.09 ± 0.027 μm/s, N ≥ 50 plasmids, p < 0.001) than in wild-type cells (0.05 ± 0.019 μm/s; Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from time-lapse microscopy experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Non-chromosomal DNA circles and NPCs reciprocally constrain the diffusion speed of each other, in a SAGA-dependent manner.
source: Thus, our data establish that non-chromosomal DNA circles and NPCs reciprocally constrain the diffusion speed of each other, in a SAGA-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the speed measurements.

claim: A large majority of aged cells showed a non-uniform distribution of NPCs on the nuclear surface.
source: Strikingly, a large majority of the aged cells showed a non-uniform distribution of NPCs on the nuclear surface. A substantial fraction of very old cells formed an even more intense cap (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Cap formation was observed upon ageing in wild-type cells.
source: Thus, cap formation was observed upon ageing in wild-type cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the aging experiments.

claim: For all three NPC markers (Nup49, Nup170, Nup82), fluorescence intensity increased significantly in the mother nuclei with age.
source: For all three NPC markers, fluorescence intensity increased significantly in the mother nuclei with age (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: The fraction of nuclear pores that segregated towards the mother cell during mitosis increased as the cells aged.
source: Accordingly, the fraction of nuclear pores that segregated towards the mother cell during mitosis increased as the cells aged, indicating that these cells partitioned NPCs in an increasingly asymmetric manner (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Young mother cells expressing Nup170-GFP retained 56 ± 1.9% of the NPC signal in the mother cell.
source: Young mother cells expressing Nup170-GFP or Nup82-GFP retained 56 ± 1.9% and 57 ± 2.5% of the signal in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from microfluidic aging experiments.

claim: Young mother cells expressing Nup82-GFP retained 57 ± 2.5% of the NPC signal in the mother cell.
source: Young mother cells expressing Nup170-GFP or Nup82-GFP retained 56 ± 1.9% and 57 ± 2.5% of the signal in the mother cell.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from microfluidic aging experiments.

claim: The retention of pores in the mother cell increased to 73 ± 5.0% after 25 generations (Nup82-GFP) and 78 ± 3.8% after 35 generations (Nup170-GFP).
source: The retention of pores in the mother cell increased after 25 generations to 73 ± 5.0% (Nup82-GFP) and 78 ± 3.8% after 35 generations (Nup170-GFP; Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Old mothers contained more NPCs than young cells (on average 4.7 ± 1.2-fold more for Nup49-GFP after 25 generations, 4.0 ± 1.1-fold for Nup170-GFP after 30 generations, and 4.1 ± 1.4-fold for Nup82-GFP after 35 generations).
source: Analysis of nuclei in G1 cells of increasing age confirmed that old mothers contained more NPCs than young cells (on average 4.7 ± 1.2-fold more than young mothers in cells expressing Nup49-GFP after 25 generations, 4.0 ± 1.1-fold in Nup170-GFP expressing cells after 30 generations, and 4.1 ± 1.4-fold in Nup82-GFP expressing cells after 35 generations; Figure 9E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Old nuclei were both larger (radius = 1.5 fold larger) and more densely populated with pores (1.9-fold increase in density) compared to the nuclei of young cells.
source: These nuclei were both larger (radius = 1.5 fold larger; Figure 9F) and more densely populated with pores (1.9-fold increase in density; Figure 9G) compared to the nuclei of young cells.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to figures.

claim: The increase with age in NPC asymmetry, NPC retention, and NPC number was much slower in cells lacking a diffusion barrier (bud6∆ mutant cells).
source: Remarkably, the increase with age in NPC asymmetry, NPC retention, and NPC number was much slower in cells lacking a diffusion barrier (bud6∆ mutant cells; Figure 9C–E).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to figures.

claim: Mother cells retain an increased number of NPCs as they age, in a diffusion barrier-dependent manner.
source: Thus, consistent with the possibility that ERC accumulation affects NPC segregation, mother cells retain an increased number of NPCs as they age, in a diffusion barrier-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the aging experiments.

claim: The proportion of NPCs retained in the mother cell at mitosis and the total amount of pores in G1 cells increased much slower with age in fob1∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type.
source: Remarkably, the proportion of NPCs retained in the mother cell at mitosis and the total amount of pores in G1 cells increased much slower with age in fob1∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type, irrespective of the reporter used (Nup49-GFP or Nup170-GFP), and faster in the sir2∆ mutant mother cells (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to figures.

claim: The proportion of NPCs retained in the mother cell at mitosis and the total amount of pores in G1 cells increased faster with age in sir2∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type.
source: Remarkably, the proportion of NPCs retained in the mother cell at mitosis and the total amount of pores in G1 cells increased much slower with age in fob1∆ mutant cells compared to wild-type, irrespective of the reporter used (Nup49-GFP or Nup170-GFP), and faster in the sir2∆ mutant mother cells (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to figures.

claim: The presence of ERCs largely drives NPC retention in ageing cells.
source: Thus, the presence of ERCs largely drives NPC retention in ageing cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fob1∆ and sir2∆ aging experiments.

claim: The sgf73∆ mutant cells accumulated NPCs slowly as they aged.
source: Consistent with the SAGA-dependent effect of non-centromeric DNA circles on pore segregation in young cells, the sgf73∆ mutant cells accumulated NPCs slowly as they aged (Figure 10A–C).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to figures.

claim: Artificially linking SAGA to NPCs using the Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 fusion proteins restored NPC accumulation in ageing sgf73∆ mutant cells.
source: Furthermore, artificially linking SAGA to NPCs using the Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 fusion proteins restored NPC accumulation in ageing sgf73∆ mutant cells (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is an observation from microfluidic aging experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: SAGA mediates the interaction of ERCs and NPCs, leading to the joined retention and accumulation of both ERCs and NPCs in ageing yeast mother cells.
source: Based on these and our findings above, we conclude that SAGA mediates the interaction of ERCs and NPCs, leading to the joined retention and accumulation of both ERCs and NPCs in ageing yeast mother cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the aging experiments.

claim: Wild-type cells showed a median lifespan of 27 generations.
source: Wild-type cells showed a median lifespan of 27 generations, whereas the sgf73∆ mutant cells lived 60% longer, (44 generations, N = 150 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 11A (Schleit et al., 2013)).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: The sgf73∆ mutant cells lived 60% longer than wild-type (44 generations).
source: Wild-type cells showed a median lifespan of 27 generations, whereas the sgf73∆ mutant cells lived 60% longer, (44 generations, N = 150 cells, p < 0.001; Figure 11A (Schleit et al., 2013)).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: gcn5∆ and spt20∆ mutant cells did not show an increased longevity (27 and 17 generations).
source: Strikingly, gcn5∆ and spt20∆ mutant cells did not show an increased longevity (27 and 17 generations, N = 50–150 cells; Figure 11A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Removal of Fob1 failed to extend the lifespan of the gcn5∆ mutant cells (median lifespan of gcn5∆ fob1∆ double mutant cells = 27 generations).
source: Accordingly, removal of Fob1 failed to extend the lifespan of the gcn5∆ mutant cells (median lifespan of gcn5∆ fob1∆ double mutant cells = 27 generations, N = 150 cells; Figure 11B) and spt20∆ mutant cells (spt20∆ fob1∆ = 16 generations, N = 75 cells; Figure 11C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Removal of Fob1 failed to extend the lifespan of the spt20∆ mutant cells (spt20∆ fob1∆ = 16 generations).
source: Accordingly, removal of Fob1 failed to extend the lifespan of the gcn5∆ mutant cells (median lifespan of gcn5∆ fob1∆ double mutant cells = 27 generations, N = 150 cells; Figure 11B) and spt20∆ mutant cells (spt20∆ fob1∆ = 16 generations, N = 75 cells; Figure 11C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Cells lacking Gcn5 and Spt20 age through mechanisms independent of ERC formation and accumulation.
source: Decreased ERC accumulation in gcn5Δ mutant cells, as suggested by our Southern Blot experiments, and in gcn5Δ fob1Δ double mutant cells did not prolong lifespan of these cells, suggesting that these cells die of reasons independent of ERC accumulation. Additionally, the fact that we observed increased ERC formation in cells lacking Gcn5 (Figure 3D) but not a shorter lifespan suggests that indeed the increased ERC formation is compensated by poor circle retention in the mother cells. Thus, cells lacking Gcn5 and Spt20 age through mechanisms independent of ERC formation and accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lifespan and ERC experiments.

claim: Expression of the fusion proteins Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 did not alter the longevity of the wild-type cells (27 generations).
source: Expression of the fusion proteins Gcn5-Sac3 and Spt7-Nup49 did not alter the longevity of the wild-type cells (27 generations, N = 50 cells; Figure 11D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Expression of Gcn5-Sac3 substantially shortened the lifespan of the sgf73∆ mutant cells (16 generations).
source: However, it substantially shortened the lifespan of the sgf73∆ mutant cells (16 and 34 generations, respectively, N ≥ 50 cells, p < 0.01; Figure 11E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Expression of Spt7-Nup49 substantially shortened the lifespan of the sgf73∆ mutant cells (34 generations).
source: However, it substantially shortened the lifespan of the sgf73∆ mutant cells (16 and 34 generations, respectively, N ≥ 50 cells, p < 0.01; Figure 11E).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from lifespan experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Decreased levels of SAGA at pores largely contribute to the extended lifespan observed in sgf73∆ cells.
source: Therefore, we conclude that decreased levels of SAGA at pores largely contribute to the extended lifespan observed in sgf73∆ cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fusion protein lifespan experiments.

claim: SAGA promotes ageing, at least in part, through promoting the anchorage of non-chromosomal DNA circles to NPCs and promoting their joint retention and accumulation with age.
source: Based on the data presented here, we further conclude that SAGA promotes ageing, at least in part, through promoting the anchorage of non-chromosomal DNA circles to NPCs and promoting their joint retention and accumulation with age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experiments.

claim: Non-chromosomal DNA circles alone do not accumulate and do not promote ageing if they are not at NPCs.
source: Furthermore, non-chromosomal DNA circles alone do not accumulate and do not promote ageing if they are not at NPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experiments.

claim: Both morpho-kinetic parameters and tethering to NPCs are required for efficient circle retention in vivo.
source: First, we propose that both morpho-kinetic parameters (Gehlen et al., 2011) as well as tethering to NPCs are required for efficient circle retention in vivo.
evidence: This is a proposed model in the discussion with citation.

claim: Tight confinement of the circles by the diffusion barrier requires the attachment of the circles to NPCs.
source: Second, we propose that tight confinement of the circles by the diffusion barrier requires the attachment of the circles to NPCs.
evidence: This is a proposed model in the discussion.

claim: What the barrier efficiently retains in the mother cell is neither NPCs alone nor the unbound circles but rather the circle-bound NPCs.
source: Indeed, what the barrier efficiently retains in the mother cell is neither NPCs alone nor the unbound circles but rather the circle-bound NPCs.
evidence: This is a proposed model in the discussion.
